summary: Describes a mechanism to carry IPv4 packets across an IPv6 network by encapsulation. It also describes a generic way to map between IPv6 addresses and IPv4 addresses and ports.

plainLanguage.summary: MAP-E lets old-style IPv4 traffic travel over a new-style IPv6 network. It also lets several sites share a single IPv4 address, because each site is given its own slice of the port numbers.

questions: mapping of address and port encapsulation
how does map-e share ipv4 addresses
subtitle: Carries IPv4 traffic across an IPv6 network and shares one IPv4 address between many sites by dividing the port space.

tldr.problem: Networks that have moved to IPv6 still have IPv4 hosts to serve, and IPv4 address space is short. Many sites also need one public IPv4 address each, which is hard to find.
tldr.mechanism: MAP-E puts IPv4 packets inside IPv6 packets and defines a rule that maps an IPv4 address and port to an IPv6 address. Sites that share an IPv4 address get separate ranges of ports, and the mapping rule says which range belongs to which site.
tldr.outcome: A service provider can give many sites one IPv4 address and still reach the public IPv4 Internet from them. The RFC is a Proposed Standard from July 2015 and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 7597 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2015. It has not been obsoleted and nothing in the unit metadata updates it, so it remains the definition of the MAP-E mechanism. Its DHCPv6 options are specified separately in RFC 7598.

sections.title: Carrying IPv4 Across IPv6
sections.content:
Putting IPv4 addresses inside IPv6 addresses has a long history, going back to the mid-1990s. The original automatic tunneling mechanism combined a host's IPv4 address with a well-known IPv6 prefix, so a node could tunnel a packet by extracting the IPv4 endpoint from the IPv6 destination address. Later variants include 6over4, 6to4, ISATAP and 6rd.

All of those share three properties: automatic provisioning of an IPv6 address for a host or an IPv6 prefix for a site, algorithmic resolution of tunnel endpoint addresses, and embedding of an IPv4 address or part of one in an IPv6 address.

This document describes the opposite direction, IPv4 over IPv6, which is what a network needs in the later phases of migration, when IPv6-only networks are common but IPv4 services still have to reach the Internet. It describes the delivery of IPv4 unicast service across an IPv6 infrastructure; IPv4 multicast is not considered. The scheme supports encapsulation of IPv4 in IPv6 in both mesh and hub-and-spoke topologies, including address mappings with full independence between IPv6 and IPv4 addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: Earlier schemes carried IPv6 traffic over IPv4. This one does the reverse: it puts IPv4 packets inside IPv6 packets so that sites which have already moved to IPv6 can still serve IPv4 users.

sections.title: The Names Used Here
sections.content:
A MAP domain is one or more Customer Edge devices and Border Relays connected to the same virtual link. A service provider may deploy a single MAP domain or several. A MAP node is any device that implements MAP.

The MAP Border Relay (BR) is a MAP-enabled router managed by the service provider at the edge of a MAP domain. It has at least an IPv6-enabled interface and an IPv4 interface connected to the native IPv4 network. The MAP Customer Edge (CE) functions as a customer edge router; a typical one serves a residential site with one WAN-side interface and one or more LAN-side interfaces.

A Port Set ID (PSID) algorithmically identifies a set of ports exclusively assigned to a CE. A shared IPv4 address is an IPv4 address shared among multiple CEs, where only ports belonging to the assigned port set can be used for communication; it is also known as a port-restricted IPv4 address. The End-user IPv6 prefix is the IPv6 prefix assigned to a CE by means other than MAP itself, and it is unique for each CE. The MAP IPv6 address is the address used to reach the MAP function of a CE from other CEs and from Border Relays.

The Embedded Address (EA) bits are the bits in the IPv6 address that identify an IPv4 prefix or address, or part of one, or a shared IPv4 address, together with a Port Set Identifier.
sections.plainLanguage: Two kinds of device take part. The customer edge router sits at the site, and the border relay sits at the edge of the provider's network and connects to the ordinary IPv4 Internet. Each site is given its own set of port numbers so that sites can share one IPv4 address.

sections.title: How the Pieces Fit Together
sections.content:
MAP reuses existing building blocks. The Network Address and Port Translator (NAPT) on the CE is used, with added support for restricting transport-protocol ports, ICMP identifiers and fragment identifiers to the configured port set. For packets sent from the private IPv4 network, the CE NAPT MUST translate transport identifiers, such as TCP and UDP port numbers, so that they fall within the CE's assigned port range. The NAPT is connected to a MAP-aware forwarding function that does the encapsulation and decapsulation of IPv4 packets in IPv6, using the encapsulation mode specified in RFC 2473.

The architecture restricts a shared IPv4 address to being the global address, outside, of the NAPT running on the CE. A shared IPv4 address MUST NOT be used to identify an interface. For full IPv4 addresses and IPv4 prefixes the same design applies with two differences: the address or prefix can be used as it is today, for example to identify an interface or as a DHCP pool, and the NAPT is not required to restrict the ports used on outgoing packets.
sections.plainLanguage: Each site keeps its usual address translation router. The MAP part sits next to it and wraps outgoing IPv4 packets in IPv6 before sending them across the provider's IPv6 network.

sections.title: The Mapping Rules
sections.content:
Every MAP node is provisioned with one or more mapping rules. Every MAP node must be provisioned with a Basic Mapping Rule (BMR), used to configure its IPv4 address, prefix or shared address. It can also be used for forwarding, mapping an IPv4 destination address and optionally a destination port into an IPv6 address. Additional rules allow several IPv4 subnets to exist inside the domain and make forwarding between them more efficient.

There can only be one Basic Mapping Rule per End-user IPv6 prefix, though all CEs whose End-user IPv6 prefixes fall within the same Rule IPv6 prefix may share one. The Forwarding Mapping Rule (FMR) is optional and used for forwarding in mesh mode; given a destination IPv4 address and port inside the domain, a node uses the matching FMR to derive the End-user IPv6 address of the interface that can reach it. In hub-and-spoke mode there are no FMRs and all traffic goes to the Border Relay.

Both kinds of rule share the same parameters: the Rule IPv6 prefix with its length, the Rule IPv4 prefix with its length, and the length of the EA bit field in bits. A node finds its BMR by longest match between its End-user IPv6 prefix and the Rule IPv6 prefixes in the table.
sections.plainLanguage: A rule is a short description of how to compute addresses. The basic rule tells a site what IPv4 address to use. The forwarding rule tells the network where to send a packet so that it reaches the right site directly.

sections.title: Dividing the Port Space
sections.content:
The port-mapping algorithm is used in domains whose rules allow IPv4 address sharing. A port range is written in a notation similar to CIDR: the first 256 ports are port prefix 0.0/8 and the last 256 ports are 255.0/8, which in hexadecimal are 0x0000/8 and 0xFF00/8, with Port Set Identifiers of 0 and 0xFF.

When the PSID is embedded in the End-user IPv6 prefix, the RFC uses an infix representation of the port value so that the well-known ports can be excluded by restricting the high-order bit field rather than the PSID. The infix algorithm allocates ports to a CE as a series of contiguous ranges spaced at regular intervals through the complete range of possible port-set values.

The port field has four parts: a bits of offset, the PSID, and m bits for the specific port. The number of offset bits is 6 by default, because that excludes the system ports 0 to 1023, and the offset MUST be the same for every CE sharing an address. The field A selects the range of the port number and, for a greater than 0, MUST be larger than 0, which is what excludes the system ports. A smaller value of a excludes a larger initial range, so a of 4 excludes ports 0 to 4095. The interval between the initial port numbers of successive ranges assigned to the same user is 2 to the power of 16 minus a.

The length k of the PSID field MUST be the same for every CE sharing the same address, and the sharing ratio is 2 to the power of k. The number of ports assigned to the user is 2 to the power of 16 minus k, minus the 2 to the power of m excluded ports.
sections.plainLanguage: Sharing one IPv4 address means sharing one list of port numbers. The RFC lays the port number out so that each site gets its own scattered set of ports, and so that the low, well-known ports stay out of the way.

sections.title: The MAP IPv6 Address
sections.content:
The complete MAP IPv6 address is built from the Rule IPv6 prefix, the EA bits, a subnet identifier and an interface identifier. The Rule IPv6 prefix is common to all CEs using the same Basic Mapping Rule. The EA bit field encodes the CE-specific IPv4 address and port information and can hold a full or partial IPv4 address and, in the shared address case, a PSID. An EA bit field length of 0 means that all relevant IPv4 addressing information is passed directly in the BMR and is not derived from the address.

Three values are defined: r is the length of the IPv4 prefix given by the BMR, o is the length of the EA bit field, and p is the length of the IPv4 suffix contained in the EA bits. The length r may be zero, in which case the complete IPv4 address or prefix is encoded in the EA bits. The offset of the EA bit field in the IPv6 address equals the BMR Rule IPv6 prefix length, and the length o can be between 0 and 48. A length of 48 means that the complete IPv4 address and port are embedded in the End-user IPv6 prefix, with a single port assigned, and a length of 0 means no part of the IPv4 address or port is embedded.

If o plus r is less than 32 an IPv4 prefix is assigned. If o plus r equals 32, a full IPv4 address is assigned, created by concatenating the Rule IPv4 prefix and the EA bits. If o plus r is greater than 32, a shared IPv4 address is assigned: the number of IPv4 suffix bits in the EA bits is 32 minus r, and the PSID bits are used to create a port set, with the length of the PSID field given by q equals o minus p.

The interface identifier format of a MAP node places 16 zero bits, then the 32-bit IPv4 address, then the 16-bit PSID. For an IPv4 prefix the address field is right-padded with zeros, and the PSID field is left-padded with zeros. For an IPv4 prefix or a complete IPv4 address the PSID field is zero.
sections.plainLanguage: The IPv6 address of a site carries the site-specific part of its IPv4 identity: some of the IPv4 address, and in the shared case the identifier of its port set. The rule tells every device how many bits to read and where.

sections.title: Forwarding and Receiving
sections.content:
IPv4 traffic between MAP nodes inside one domain is encapsulated in IPv6, with the sender's MAP IPv6 address as the source and the receiving node's MAP IPv6 address as the destination. Traffic to IPv4 destinations outside the domain is also encapsulated, but the destination IPv6 address is set to the configured IPv6 address of the Border Relay. A typical CE router installs a default IPv4 route to the BR.

For a shared IPv4 address, a CE forwarding IPv4 packets from the LAN performs NAT44 functions first and creates the matching bindings. The resulting packets MUST contain the source IPv4 address and source transport identifiers specified by the MAP provisioning parameters, and the IPv6 source and destination addresses are derived from the mapping rule. On the receiving side, a CE sends an IPv6 packet addressed to its MAP IPv6 address to its MAP function, where it is decapsulated and handed to the NAT44 function.

To prevent spoofing of IPv4 addresses, every MAP node MUST validate received packets. It extracts the embedded IPv4 address or prefix and the PSID from the source IPv6 address using the matching rule, extracts the source IPv4 address and port from the encapsulated IPv4 packet, and if the latter fall outside the acceptable range the packet MUST be silently discarded and a counter incremented. These checks are not done for packets whose source IPv6 address is that of the Border Relay. By default the CE router MUST drop packets received on the MAP virtual interface for IPv4 destinations that are not its own.
sections.plainLanguage: Packets inside the domain go straight from site to site. Packets heading for the rest of the IPv4 Internet go to the border relay. Every receiver checks that the IPv4 address inside the packet matches the one carried in the IPv6 address, and drops the packet if it does not.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC discusses four areas. On spoofing, with consistency checks between the IPv4 and IPv6 sources performed on packets received by MAP nodes, MAP does not introduce any new opportunity for spoofing attacks that would not already exist in IPv6.

On denial of service, in domains where IPv4 addresses are shared, the fact that IPv4 datagram reassembly may be necessary introduces an opportunity for denial-of-service attacks. This is inherent in address sharing and is common with other address-sharing approaches such as DS-Lite and NAT64/DNS64. The best protection is to accelerate IPv6 deployment so that address sharing is used less and less.

On routing loops, these may exist in some automatic tunneling scenarios, but they cannot exist with MAP because each BR checks that the IPv6 source address of a received packet is a CE address based on the Forwarding Mapping Rule.

On attacks facilitated by a restricted port set, a host that is not subject to ingress filtering can inject spoofed packets during ongoing transport connections. The attacks depend on guessing which ports are currently used by target hosts. To minimize them, the CE's NAT44 filtering behavior SHOULD be Address-Dependent Filtering, and the CEs SHOULD use a DNS transport proxy function to handle DNS traffic from IPv6 interfaces that are not assigned to MAP.
sections.plainLanguage: MAP does not add new ways to fake an address, because each receiver checks the two addresses against each other. Sharing one address does mean some attacks on packet reassembly become possible, and it makes guessing which ports a host is using easier, so the RFC asks for tighter filtering rules.
